```{.quiz-yaml}
id: 17_correlation_pairs
title: What do we do with the numbers?
questions:
  - id: above_average
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      Think about someone who spent a lot more on others than the average
      person in the sample. If spending on others really does go with being
      happier, where would you expect their happiness to be, compared with
      the average?
    options:
      - text: Above average
        correct: true
      - text: Below average
      - text: Close to average
      - text: There's no way to tell
    explanation: >
      Probably above average. We can't be sure about any one person, but if
      the two variables go together, being high on one should tend to go
      with being high on the other.

  - id: below_average
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      Now think about someone who spent a lot *less* on others than the
      average person. Where would you expect their happiness to be, compared
      with the average?
    options:
      - text: Above average
      - text: Below average
        correct: true
      - text: Close to average
      - text: There's no way to tell
    explanation: >
      Probably below average. It's the same pattern from the other direction:
      low on one variable tends to go with low on the other. So this person
      and the one in the last question have something in common. Each is on
      the same side of the average for both variables.

  - id: close_to_average
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      What about someone who spent about the same as the average person?
      Where would you expect their happiness to be, compared with the
      average?
    options:
      - text: Above average
      - text: Below average
      - text: Close to average
        correct: true
      - text: There's no way to tell
    explanation: >
      Probably somewhere close to average. If their spending is right in the
      middle, it doesn't point either way. That also means people like this
      don't tell us much about whether the two variables go together. It's
      the people far from average who show the pattern most clearly.

  - id: one_number
    type: free-response
    checkLabel: Save response
    prompt: >
      Any ideas how we might turn this idea into a single number that
      describes the whole sample? You don't need a formula; just jot down an
      idea.
    explanation: >
      One way would be to count how many people are on the same side of both
      averages (above average on both, or below average on both), and how
      many are on opposite sides. If the two variables had nothing to do with
      each other, those counts should come out roughly even. As we'll see,
      that's very close to the idea behind the correlation statistic. And as
      the last question suggested, we might also want people far from
      average to count for more than people close to it.
```
